description:
Team ZeroGravity is a group of Computer Science & Engineering students from Jashore University of Science and Technology (JUST), Bangladesh. We joined the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to apply our software and AI skills to a real problem in human spaceflight. 

For a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, we researched NASA resources, designed an educational lunar-outpost simulation, and built an interactive platform that helps young learners understand how interconnected engineering decisions affect crew safety, resources, and mission success.
summary: LunaQuest is a browser-based junior astronaut mission simulator that lets young learners command a four-person lunar outpost over up to 30 simulated days. Players spend a fixed 100-credit budget across seven interconnected systems — solar arrays, battery storage, oxygen generation, water recycling, greenhouse, radiation shielding and emergency reserves — then advance one day at a time, making real decisions during solar storms, water leaks and power faults. The simulation engine runs the same physics-based resource model in every preview and every playthrough, so every number students see comes from the same verifiable rules. Live NASA DONKI space-weather data sets the severity of in-game solar storms, and a Science Lab module links every engineering choice to a real NASA reference.
details:
LunaQuest answers the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer by turning a lunar life-support engineering problem into an interactive decision loop that any curious student can follow in a browser.

How it works:

The core is a pure TypeScript simulation engine that models one mission day at a time. Each day, oxygen, water, food and battery charge change by rates derived from real life-support figures (0.84 kg O₂ · 3 L water · 1.8 kg food per astronaut per day; electrolysis at the 8:1 oxygen-to-hydrogen mass ratio). Solar output follows an illustrative illumination profile that includes a terrain-shadow dip mid-mission. Random emergencies - solar storms, power faults, water leaks, crop failures -arrive from a seeded generator; each one presents three choices, each with a live consequence preview calculated by the same engine before the player commits. A Zustand store persists the full mission state to localStorage so players can resume across sessions.

The site has six main screens:

1. Landing — explains the loop in four interactive steps, an animated live simulation preview, and a zero-sum budget demo.

2. Mission Selection — Moon (four scenarios, fully playable) and Mars (designed but locked, shown as the stretch goal).

3. Briefing → Configure — players pick a scenario and allocate their 100-credit budget across seven systems with a live 30-day resource projection updating as they spend.

4. Mission Control — resource strip with real-time gauges, outpost schematic, telemetry chart, emergency decision dialogs with choice previews, power switches (air / water recycling / grow lights / science), bonus spacewalk and reinforced shelter actions.

5. Timeline — interactive Recharts graph of all resources across the mission, event inspector and mission log.

6. Debrief — scored across four axes (crew safety, science objectives, resource margins, emergency response) with an explanation of exactly how each sub-score was calculated.

A seventh screen, the Science Lab, has seven short modules — life support, radiation, energy, water, food, habitat engineering and trade-offs - each showing the game model, the real-world practice, and the simplification made.

The Sources & Data page lists every source with its kind (NASA data, NASA reference, simplified assumption or game rule), what it is used for in the game, and what the game cannot do with it. The NASA DONKI live status is shown in real time.

The challenge it answers:

Junior learners rarely encounter the idea that systems thinking - not just individual facts - is what keeps a space crew alive. By giving students a fixed budget and letting them live with the consequences of every choice across 12–30 simulated days, LunaQuest makes abstract engineering trade-offs visible and personal. The communication delay feature (2.6 s Moon round-trip to "Ask Mission Control"; one-day delay for the Mars-distance drill) adds the real constraint that decision-making in space is intentionally independent.

What we'd build next:

- Full Mars Outpost scenario (designed; engine data model already includes it).

- Dust-storm and thin-atmosphere events specific to Mars.

- Teacher dashboard: class-wide mission log, aggregate decision statistics.

- Localisation into Bangla and additional languages for accessibility.

- Learning-outcomes study with student cohorts to measure retention of life-support concepts.

- Fission surface power as an unlockable upgrade in the First Lunar Night scenario (replacing solar during the dark period, as NASA's own Fission Surface Power project proposes).
